title: Runtime Trust Compact: concise positioning for builders and platform buyers
content:
Runtime Trust Compact

One-line positioning: Redwood is the runtime teams trust to turn large language models into predictable, cost-effective, and resilient services — the place engineers go when model quality alone isn’t enough.

Why this brief exists
- Short, operational messaging for field + product teams who need a compact explanation of what Redwood stands for and why engineering buyers choose us.
- Focus: ‘runtime trust’ — not just model access, but turning models into reliable production services with predictable economics and controllable risk.

Core problem we solve
- Models are getting better but are fragile in production. Teams face three recurring gaps: 1) unpredictable latency and cost as traffic scales, 2) brittle fallbacks and degraded user experience when capacity or region fails, 3) fragmented tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments that makes the path to production slow and risky.

Thesis (2 sentences)
- The strategic advantage has shifted from owning models to owning the runtime that serves them. Customers win by treating inference as a service problem — predictable latency, measurable unit economics, and operational controls.
- Redwood provides that runtime: high-throughput serving, deterministic fallbacks, transparent unit economics, and one consistent API across hosted, reserved, and private footprints.

Why Redwood (3 pillars)
1) Predictability by design — engineering-first SLAs and observable token-level economics
   - What it means: latency SLOs, per-route cost/latency breakdowns, and simple knobs that guarantee tail-latency under mixed workloads.
   - Proof signals: benchmarked tail latencies across common open models, customer examples where cost variance dropped >35% after adopting Redwood Optimize recommendations.

2) Cost control without sacrificing quality — runtime levers that give concrete unit-economics wins
   - What it means: automatic batching, KV/prefix caching, model variant routing, and quantization profiles tuned by workload.
   - Proof signals: suggested batching/caching reduced median tokens/sec cost by ~20–40% in internal perf tests for chat workloads.

3) Deployment versatility with a single contract — same API, same tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private
   - What it means: customers can start on hosted API, move to Dedicated for committed throughput, and deploy Private behind their VPC without rewriting integrations.
   - Proof signals: customers migrated from hosted to Dedicated with <3% code delta and consistent SLOs.

Primary buyer personas and one-line hooks
- Product/ML engineer (builder): "Ship fast. Keep latency and cost predictable."
- Platform/Infra lead (platform buyer): "Standardize inference across teams with SLAs and cost controls."
- Security/Compliance manager (enterprise buyer): "Run inference under our network and policy controls while keeping operational visibility."

Message hierarchy (short -> leading -> supporting)
- Short: "A runtime teams trust for production LLMs."
- Leading: "Redwood converts model capability into predictable service-level outcomes — latency, cost, and reliability — across any deployment mode."
- Supporting bullets: deterministic fallbacks, token-level cost transparency, model variant routing, KV cache and batching, one API for hosted/dedicated/private.

Concrete differentiators vs typical competitors
- Managed model-access APIs: They surface models; we ship service-level economics and operational primitives. We measure and control the unit cost drivers, not just tokens generated.
- Cloud endpoint offerings: Those give VMs and scaling but leave serving optimizations to the customer. Redwood ships an inference runtime that picks kernels, batches intelligently, and preserves SLOs out of the box.
- Self-hosted runtimes: They provide control but require building ops, autoscaling, and observability. Redwood packages that operational burden with optional Dedicated and Private modes and an enterprise SLA.

Short battlecards (objection -> response)
- Objection: "We can just use a cloud managed endpoint or host open-source models ourselves."
  Response: "Those paths work until variability in workload and tail-latency hits your users or costs spike. Redwood reduces that variability with runtime-level controls and observable economics — saving both engineering time and dollars at scale."

- Objection: "We can fold performance work into our infra roadmap."
  Response: "You can, but replacing a one-off infra project with a product that continuously tunes batching, caching, and kernels gives sustained cost wins and fewer regressions — freeing your team to ship features, not ops fixes."

- Objection: "We need on-prem / air-gapped deployments for compliance."
  Response: "Redwood Private is designed for those constraints — same API and rollout semantics, integrated KMS/HSM and audit trails, and a support+SLA model for enterprise operations."

Examples: 6–12 second elevator pitches
- For builders: "Redwood is the inference runtime your app uses to make models behave like production services — predictable latency, transparent cost, and safe fallbacks — so you can ship features with confidence."
- For platform leads: "Redwood standardizes how your org runs LLMs: one API, per-route SLOs, and observability that makes chargeback, rollout, and incident analysis frictionless."

Proof points to cite in calls and decks (short form)
- "Benchmark: 95th percentile latency reduced by X–Y% vs baseline for common chat workloads in our internal tests."
- "Customer: reduced per-token cost variance by 35% after batching + cache recommendations."
- "Enterprise: Private deploys with KMS integration and 12-month platform SLA."

Suggested assets and rapid experiments to produce now
- One-pager: ‘runtime trust checklist’ — observable metrics every platform leader should demand.
- Scripted demo: live demo showing behavior under load (fail region, fallback to variant model).
- Benchmark kit: reproducible benchmark recipe for common chat and embedding workloads with baseline configs.

Activation plan for early GTM (30/60/90)
- 30 days: equip SDRs and AEs with two-line hooks + 1-pager; run internal playbook rehearsal.
- 60 days: create benchmark kit + scripted demo and publish on developer docs + community blog.
- 90 days: run outreach to platform engineering meetup lists and targeted accounts with demo + proof deck.

Success metrics (what GTM measures)
- Short-term: demo-to-PoC conversion rate (target: 20% higher than prior baseline).
- Mid-term: reduction in customer-reported tail-latency incidents after onboarding (target: measurable reduction within 60 days).
- Long-term: ARR from Dedicated/Private motions and churn of Hosted customers moving to Dedicated with renewed contracts.

Implementation notes for product and docs teams
- Emphasize observability screenshots that show token-level cost and tail-latency on the same timeline.
- Produce a short technical appendix describing batching, KV cache semantics, and model variant routing in plain language for architects.
- Keep customer stories concrete: numbers and before/after comparisons matter more than adjectives.

Tone guidance
- Direct, technical, outcome-oriented. Avoid vague claims about being the "best" model access — emphasize predictable service-level outcomes and measurable economic levers.

Open questions to resolve (owner + due dates)
- Benchmark publicization policy: which internal test results can we publish? (Owner: Marco; due: 2025-03-10)
- Standardized demo script: who owns the failover demo? (Owner: Hannah; due: 2025-03-01)
- Proof point collection: top 3 customers willing to share metrics? (Owner: Leo; due: 2025-03-15)

Appendix: short FAQ
Q: Does Redwood replace model selection?
A: No. Redwood complements model selection. We help you run chosen models as services — reducing friction, cost, and operational risk.

Q: How do deployments differ across modes?
A: API and rollout semantics are consistent. Hosted is fastest to onboard; Dedicated provides committed throughput/SLAs; Private gives network/control surface required by regulated workloads.

Q: How do we quantify cost savings?
A: Start with unit tests: run sample workload with baseline config and with Redwood Optimize suggestions. Track token-level cost decomposition and per-request latency percentiles. Report delta.

— end of brief —

Notes: This compact is intended to be a living short-form narrative for quick GTM enablement. Use for call scripts, slides, and product blurbs; for longer stories, expand into a full messaging guide with customer case studies and technical appendices.
